> "Node soup is answered by Shneiderman's *"overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand"* — thin nodes, detail in an inspector, edge labels only near focus. On diffing, the **tornado diagram** is canonical, sorted by absolute impact, **7–12 bars being readable** — and **a tornado bar is exactly a conditional-pair spread**, so the sorted-spread chart is a payoff screen, not a side panel. The best interactive finance precedent is the Minneapolis Fed's stress-test tool: preset scenarios with select-all overlay, a few toggles, overlaid trajectories against a fixed red threshold line, small multiples of drivers underneath."

Also on layout stability: "crossing minimisation is NP-hard, so **stability beats optimality**: animate layout changes, preserve pinned positions, never reflow the whole canvas on a small edit."

## 2G. Time-to-first-output and latency tolerance (§3 line 43, §3 line 45, §4 lines 57, 55, §7 line 106)

Latency named as a judged criterion:
> "**Implicit criteria** (what gets judged in 20–40 minutes): Does a number move when I edit, and is the movement defensible? Can I *disagree* — override the model? **Is it fast enough to play with (latency is a design constraint, not an ops detail)?** Does it admit what it doesn't know? Would the output survive being pasted into an investment-committee email?…"

The demo clock — this is the file's explicit time-to-first-output expectation:
> "**The critical-path demo (5 minutes).** 0:00 type "The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week" → **0:20 a typed graph appears** (events / mechanisms / market outcomes), each node showing its probability bar → 0:40 click an edge: mechanism sentence, transmission channel, base rate with *n* and *k*, likelihood ratio, 2–3 dated citations, a counter-argument → 1:30 *"but Iran is struck the next day"* — injected as a **forced** intervention; the graph diffs against the pinned baseline with ghosted priors and the Brent distribution visibly shifts → 2:30 sensitivity shading names the one edge that actually moves the answer → 3:00 override it by hand, everything re-propagates instantly → 3:30 the **thesis card**… → 4:30 pin scenario, export."

So: **first graph on screen at 0:20**; edge detail at 0:40; every subsequent interaction effectively instant.

The architectural rule that produces that:
> "**The highest-leverage architectural decision** is separating **generation** (slow, LLM, once per graph) from **evaluation** (fast, deterministic, local, no network). **If every edit re-prompts the model you get multi-second latency, non-comparable outputs and no possible diff — the multiverse collapses into "ask again."** Parameterise the graph at generation time so edits are instant. Every pattern in §2 is downstream of this one choice."

Hard thresholds:
- §7 item 2: "**Editing is instant and local.** Re-propagation without an LLM call. **Measure it: sub-100ms, or the multiverse is fiction.**"
- §6 concept B: "every edit re-propagates **under 50ms** with the baseline ghosted behind"
- §4: engine sized at "forward propagation over a DAG with noisy-OR combination, leak terms, `do()` as edge-cutting, **5–10k Monte Carlo samples** for the terminal distribution. A few hundred lines, milliseconds in-browser."

Offline tolerance:
> "**Demo robustness is a feature:** ship a cached deterministic replay of at least the Hormuz graph. A live API call failing at minute two of a 20-minute demo is the highest-probability catastrophe in this project."

## 2H. How rivals show sources/evidence — and the porting recipe (§5, lines 69–84)

The single most relevant competitor result on evidence display:
> "AuditForecast diagnoses the problem exactly: agents *"collect evidence and discuss it in prose without an explicit update path from evidence to forecast, which limits both forecasting accuracy and auditability."* Its fix is three stages — derive a **base probability** from a reference class, identify **model-external factors**, assign each a **likelihood ratio** linked to a specific retrieved source, then combine **mechanically in odds space**. It beats stronger, costlier agents using fewer searches ([arXiv 2609.05905](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05905))."

Measured claim: **beats stronger, costlier agents using fewer searches** (no effect size given in the file). Note the convergence with research-A §3: base-rate-first, odds-space combination, mechanical rather than prose aggregation.

The per-edge evidence payload:
> "- **Claim** — a resolvable proposition, Metaculus-style: *"Brent front-month falls ≥8% within 10 sessions of reopening, per ICE settlement."* Threshold, window, source of truth.
> - **Mechanism** — one sentence with a causal verb, plus a typed **transmission channel** (physical supply, risk premium, positioning/flow, policy reaction, second-order demand). Typed channels are how you detect that two "independent" edges are the same channel double-counted.
> - **Direction, magnitude, lag** — causality takes time; Loopy's best idea.
> - **Base rate** — reference class with *n*, *k*, source, and FutureSearch's warning where it applies: *is the generating mechanism still active?*
> - **Likelihood ratio with the arithmetic visible** — prior odds × LR = posterior odds, rendered as a readable line, not a tooltip.
> - **Evidence** — 2–5 items with quote, URL, publication date and a **stance** flag (supports / contradicts). If contradicting evidence isn't representable you have rebuilt Kialo's pro-side inflation.
> - **Assumptions** — enumerated, individually toggleable.
> - **Red team** — the strongest single reason this edge fails, generated adversarially in a separate pass. DoWhy makes refutation an explicit pipeline stage ([DoWhy](https://www.pywhy.org/dowhy/)); make it an explicit *UI* stage.
> - **What would change my mind** — a named observable, a date, a source. This is also the stop-loss trigger…
> - **Provenance** — model, prompt version, retrieval timestamp, and a flag on every number the *user* overrode."

> "The matching UI affordance is a **trace**: select the terminal node, get the ordered arithmetic from anchor to answer, each term clickable back to its source. That is the literal answer to "exactly why and how to audit that.""

Note the **"challenge" verb is specified as a separate adversarial generation pass** (red team) plus **an explicit UI stage** — the file's answer to argument-mapping's pro-side inflation.

## 2I. Rubrics / human evaluation of generated reasoning (§7, lines 102–118)

The file's rubric is its §7 reviewer checklist — a 15-item human-evaluation instrument with **items 1–5 pass/fail**:

> "1. **End-to-end path exists.** Prompt → graph → edit → changed number → thesis, no manual steps, no dead ends. If engine and canvas are not joined, nothing else counts.
> 2. **Editing is instant and local.** Re-propagation without an LLM call. Measure it: sub-100ms, or the multiverse is fiction.
> 3. **A baseline is pinned and diffed.** Every modified world shown *against* the original — ghost overlay, delta badges, or side-by-side. Retired branches are annulled, not deleted.
> 4. **Every edge carries a mechanism, a base rate, and ≥2 dated citations with real URLs. Spot-check three for hallucination; contradicting evidence must be representable.**
> 5. **The thesis output is concrete.** Instrument, direction, entry, invalidation *condition*, sizing, monitoring trigger — not a paragraph of prose.
> 6. **Intervene vs. observe is distinguished.**…
> 7. **Chain probabilities are not naively multiplied.** Look for leak terms, depth caps, or anchoring. A five-deep chain returning 2% is the multiple-stage fallacy shipping.
> 8. **User override exists and is visibly attributed.** One interaction, and AI vs. human numbers stay distinguishable.
> 9. **Sensitivity is surfaced unprompted.** Graph shading first, tornado second.
> 10. **Both use cases run on the same artefact**…
> 11. **Uncertainty is a distribution, not a point.** `5 to 9`-style input is the cheapest good affordance.
> 12. **Nodes are resolvable propositions** — threshold, window, source of truth, not "oil goes down."
> 13. **Demo is robust offline** — a cached deterministic replay of the headline scenario.
> 14. **Two of the four example inputs work**, one non-geopolitical, proving the generator isn't fitted to Hormuz.
> 15. **Repo signals judgement, not ceremony**…"

Item 4 is the concrete **human evaluation protocol for generated evidence: spot-check three citations for hallucination.**

Human-evaluation budget stated in §3: "**what gets judged in 20–40 minutes**."

Under-engineering failure modes read as the inverse rubric (§4, line 61):
> "an LLM wrapper with a pretty graph and no arithmetic; numbers that don't change when you edit; **hallucinated or undated citations**; "modify event" implemented as a re-prompt; no baseline to diff against; no thesis stage…"

## 2J. The multiple-stage fallacy — bears directly on generated-chain evaluation (§2a, line 33)

> "**(a) The multiple-stage fallacy.** Decompose into six stages, multiply, and the result is almost certainly far too small — stage probabilities are correlated and people fail to condition on "everything upstream already happened" ([LW](https://www.lesswrong.com/w/multiple-stage-fallacy), [Kaufman](https://www.jefftk.com/p/multiple-stage-fallacy)). A tool that naively multiplies edge probabilities will demo a **3% answer** to "does Hormuz opening lower oil prices" and lose the room. Mitigations: cap depth; add a noisy-OR leak term for residual paths; anchor the terminal node to a base rate or market-implied level and present the chain as a **shift from that anchor**; **show the chain-derived and a direct holistic estimate side by side, surfacing disagreement rather than hiding it.**"

The last mitigation is a *display* mechanism for elicitation disagreement, and it is the direct product analogue of research-A's §3 "chain sanity" coherence check.

## 2K. Interactive verbs — the file's verdict on which ones pay (§6, lines 90–96)

> "**B — The Multiverse Scrubber.** Bet: exploration is the product. Baseline pinned; fork it; every edit re-propagates under 50ms with the baseline ghosted behind; sensitivity shading, tornado drill-down, small multiples of pinned scenarios, animated pulses along edges. *Wins* "engaging to explore" and hits the multiverse requirement dead centre. *Risk:* fast, pretty, and exactly Kumu's proof-by-intimidation failure if the audit layer is thin."

> "**Pick: B as the spine, A as detail-on-demand, C as the terminal screen.** The brief's own verbs are "explore," "modifying," "seeing downstream effects" — that is B. But B alone fails §5 and A alone fails the demo. So: the canvas is home and everything re-propagates instantly (B); clicking any edge opens the full ledger with the odds arithmetic and the red team (A); the run ends on a thesis card inheriting its invalidation conditions directly from the edges' "what would change my mind" fields (C). **These are not alternatives — they are one object at three zoom levels, and the discipline is to build the zoom-out and zoom-in *for one chain* before adding a second.**"

The verb ranking implied across the file: **edit/override** (rubric items 2, 8; "Can I *disagree* — override the model?") and **expand/inspect** (Shneiderman details-on-demand, the edge trace) are load-bearing; **challenge** must be built as an explicit adversarial pass or the map inflates (Kialo/argument-mapping warning); **add** is the cheapest verb and therefore the most dangerous one left unbalanced.

Effort allocation (§4, line 53), relevant to how much of the build goes to map generation vs. evidence vs. evaluation:
> "Allocation: **generation quality + node/edge schema 30%**, **canvas & interaction 30%**, **probability engine 15%**, **thesis output 15%**, **infra/tests 10%**."

## 5. Does anything grade CONTENT?

**No. Nothing grades content anywhere in run.py or the spec.** Precisely:

- *Is the claim resolvable?* Only the **presence** of the three fields is checked. Check 4 is the `missing_resolution` violation code (`domain/validity.py:244`) — criteria string non-empty, judge named, resolve-by date present. No check that the criteria are operational, that the named judge would actually publish a number, or that the date is sane. (`domain/validity.py` does separately enforce resolve-by > as-of date, but that is a date-ordering rule, not a content judgement.)
- *Does the source support the claim?* No. Check 3 requires a `documented` link to have a **non-empty `sources` list** (`validity.py:443`: `if link.provenance in PROVENANCE_CLAIMING_EVIDENCE and not link.sources`). Check 8 requires `base_rate.sources` to be non-empty. The strongest form of grounding anywhere is `keep_cited` in `engine/expand.py:312-319`, which drops a cited URL unless that **URL string** appeared in what the search tool returned. URL-membership, never content support.
- *Is the mechanism specific?* No. Check 3 only requires a rationale field to be non-empty (`missing_rationale`). `argued_links` counts arrows with "a mechanism and no such address" — but "mechanism" here means only that `provenance == "argued"`, a word the model chose; nothing inspects the sentence.

This is stated as policy, not oversight: `run.py:3-9` ("Not one of them is a judgement about a sentence"), `run.py:30-31` ("It will not grade a sentence, ask a model to grade one, or assert on which claim the answer named"), `evaluation.md:175` ("There is no column that requires an opinion"), anti-patterns 1, 2 and 6 (`evaluation.md:297-307`), and the not-measured table (`evaluation.md:236-245`) which explicitly excludes wording, narrative quality, whether a claim is true, and calibration.

Also: Explore cases auto-pass. | `run.py:676-719` |

## 4. `make eval` — invocation and cost

Makefile at `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst-wt/feat-04b-evals/Makefile:78-81`:

```make
eval: ## Score what the language model proposes against saved examples. Spends money; needs a key
	cd backend && PYTHONPATH=.. uv run python -m evals.run \
	  $(if $(ONLY),--only $(ONLY),) $(if $(CAP),--cap $(CAP),) \
	  $(if $(EFFORT),--effort $(EFFORT),)
```

Documented forms (`Makefile:59-62`, mirrored at `evaluation.md:200-205`): `make eval` / `ONLY=hormuz` / `CAP=5` / `EFFORT=medium`. There is deliberately **no MODEL flag** — `KATALYST_MODEL` alone (`Makefile:65-67`, `evaluation.md:207`, `run.py:33-36`).

Argparse at `run.py:1039-1058`: `--only` (default `""`), `--cap` (default `Caps().dollars` = **15.0**, `backend/src/katalyst/engine/outcome.py:326-328`), `--effort` choices `["", low, medium, high, xhigh, max]` — empty sends nothing and leaves the service default.

**Yes, it spends money.** `a_stand_in_answerer() or live_answerer(...)` at `run.py:1070`; `NO_KEY` exit 1 with no key (`run.py:81`, `1071-1073`). A stand-in run prints the table but **writes no TSV and returns 1** (`ANSWERED_BY_A_STAND_IN`, `run.py:84-88`, `1087-1089`).

**The ceiling is per case, not per round.** `ceiling = min(cap, Caps().dollars)` inside `run_one` (`run.py:354`), and `main` loops `[run_one(one, answerer=answerer, cap=said.cap) for one in wanted]` (`run.py:1076`). So a default 4-case round has a worst case of 4 × $15 = **$60**, with no round-level stop anywhere in the harness. The Makefile and spec both describe CAP as "the run's spending ceiling" (`evaluation.md:209`), which reads as per-round.

**Model calls per round — not written down anywhere as a number.** Calls are emergent from `Caps` (depth 5, width 3, claims 30, at_once 3, searches 750). The only measured figures are in `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst-wt/feat-04b-evals/docs/measurements.md`:

- 2026-09-21, Hormuz, `claude-sonnet-5`, service default effort: **34 calls, 108 searches, $4.89, 44 m 33 s** (`measurements.md:56-67`)
- same day, `EFFORT=medium`: **17 calls, 38 searches, $1.31, 7 m 46 s**
- 2026-09-17, Hormuz, `claude-opus-5`: **10 calls, 9 searches, $1.32, 10 m 54 s** (`measurements.md:132-147`) — this is the figure `evaluation.md:183` quotes as the baseline measurement that named the columns

Extrapolating (mine, not written down): one four-case round ≈ **68 calls / ~$5** at `EFFORT=medium`, ≈ **136 calls / ~$20** at default effort — which would exceed a $15 round budget if CAP were per-round.

**The only cost estimate written down** is `evaluation.md:318` (open question 2): "Kent's G5 sizes the stack at about $500 and a run at no more than $15, and estimates cassettes, four recordings, two or three re-record rounds and **about five eval rounds**. Nothing has been measured." It asks for the estimate to be redone against the first Hormuz cost before a second full round runs.

## 5. Does anything grade CONTENT?

**No. Nothing grades content anywhere in run.py or the spec.** Precisely:

- *Is the claim resolvable?* Only the **presence** of the three fields is checked. Check 4 is the `missing_resolution` violation code (`domain/validity.py:244`) — criteria string non-empty, judge named, resolve-by date present. No check that the criteria are operational, that the named judge would actually publish a number, or that the date is sane. (`domain/validity.py` does separately enforce resolve-by > as-of date, but that is a date-ordering rule, not a content judgement.)
- *Does the source support the claim?* No. Check 3 requires a `documented` link to have a **non-empty `sources` list** (`validity.py:443`: `if link.provenance in PROVENANCE_CLAIMING_EVIDENCE and not link.sources`). Check 8 requires `base_rate.sources` to be non-empty. The strongest form of grounding anywhere is `keep_cited` in `engine/expand.py:312-319`, which drops a cited URL unless that **URL string** appeared in what the search tool returned. URL-membership, never content support.
- *Is the mechanism specific?* No. Check 3 only requires a rationale field to be non-empty (`missing_rationale`). `argued_links` counts arrows with "a mechanism and no such address" — but "mechanism" here means only that `provenance == "argued"`, a word the model chose; nothing inspects the sentence.

This is stated as policy, not oversight: `run.py:3-9` ("Not one of them is a judgement about a sentence"), `run.py:30-31` ("It will not grade a sentence, ask a model to grade one, or assert on which claim the answer named"), `evaluation.md:175` ("There is no column that requires an opinion"), anti-patterns 1, 2 and 6 (`evaluation.md:297-307`), and the not-measured table (`evaluation.md:236-245`) which explicitly excludes wording, narrative quality, whether a claim is true, and calibration.

## 6. Judge / rubric / pastcast / brier / backtest / calibration

**No implementation of any of them anywhere in the worktree.** Grep over the whole tree returns only prose. The relevant hits:

- **Model-as-judge: explicitly forbidden.** `evaluation.md:239` ("Narrative quality, scored by a model — A model grading a model's prose is a number nobody computed"), anti-pattern 2 at `evaluation.md:299` ("Do not have a model grade the output … which is the one thing Kent vetoes on sight").
- **Human rubric: none.** The only human step is "a human reading a diff of two scorecards" (`evaluation.md:299`) and the PR-checklist item "prompt changed? cassettes re-recorded, `make eval` scorecard attached" (`evaluation.md:224`).
- **Pastcast / Brier: spec-only, deferred to stack 07.** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md:149` (FR-30), `evaluation.md:194`, `evaluation.md:240`, and open question 1 at `evaluation.md:317` — which lists the three missing prerequisites (resolved events with dates, a date-frozen corpus, a calibration column). Also `ARCHITECTURE.md:311` and `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md:278`. No code.
- **Calibration: deliberately absent as a column.** `evaluation.md:196`: "There is deliberately no calibration column here, because nothing in these four cases resolves." Post-hoc calibration fitting is in the out-of-scope list (`PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md:235`). The word "uncalibrated" in the frontend is a UI label on the model interval, not a measurement.
- **Backtest:** only `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md:29` (a competitor's product) and `:235` (out of scope).
- The word "judge" elsewhere is the domain sense — the named source that resolves a proposition.

## 7. Eval output

Two destinations, both written on every run regardless of score.

**The committed scorecard.** `write_tsv()` (`run.py:913-936`) writes `evals/runs/<run_at date>.tsv`, **appending** if the file exists so a second run the same day adds rows without a second header. Columns come from `COLUMNS = (*ABOUT_THE_WHOLE_RUN, *CaseScore.model_fields)` (`run.py:862`) — i.e. `run_at`, `model`, `prompt_hash` repeated on every row, then all 25 `CaseScore` fields in declaration order, 28 columns total. `_as_a_cell` (`run.py:939-951`) writes `None` as an empty cell (not the terminal's dash), ISO-formats datetimes, and replaces any tab with a space.

`evals/runs/` currently contains **only `.gitkeep`** — no scorecard has ever been committed on this branch. The `.gitkeep` file itself documents the format.

**The terminal.** `as_a_table()` (`run.py:870-890`) prints the card **transposed** — one line per field, one column per case — then `"{passed} of {n} cases held all eight checks."`, then `_how_it_went()` (`run.py:999-1018`) to stderr naming each failed check by number, name and the rules' own sentence. Exit code 0 only when `card.failed == 0`.

**The raw run.** Every case additionally writes its whole run to `backend/.runs/` via the recorder's own `keep()` (`run.py:410-425`), tagged with `EVAL_RUNS_WRITE_NO_RECORDING` (`run.py:95-97`). Not committed. Note `_closing` (`run.py:434-472`) deliberately does **not** propagate likelihoods: "a scorecard that quietly ran the engine would be measuring two things at once."

## 8. The baseline for ADR-0015 / the critique pass

`evaluation.md:116` is the load-bearing sentence:

> Kent settled on 2026-09-17 (S8) that FR-9's adversarial critique pass stays out of stack 04 — it roughly doubles the calls and its value cannot be read without something to compare it against. **So the scorecard's fields are named here, now, and the first run is the baseline stack 07 compares against.** The same applies to the ensemble that decision record 0015 said *not yet* to.

The baseline is made operational by the prediction table at `evaluation.md:189-194`:

| Candidate | Columns it should move | Columns it must not move |
|---|---|---|
| FR-9's critique pass (stack 07) | `argued_links` down, `documented_links` up, `rejected` up — and `calls`, `dollars`, `seconds` up, which is the price | `violations` and `asserted_links` (both already zero), `endings` (already at least one) |
| An ensemble (record 0015 — *not yet*) | **none of them.** An ensemble changes the *numbers on the chips*, and this scorecard deliberately scores none | everything here |

Reinforced by anti-pattern 7 (`evaluation.md:309`: "Do not score an ensemble against this scorecard … a comparison would come back flat and be read as evidence either way") and by `evaluation.md:187` ("a change is worth its money only if it moves a column somebody named in advance").

The one dated numeric baseline written down is `evaluation.md:183`: Hormuz, live, `claude-opus-5`, default effort, 2026-09-17 — **10 calls, 9 searches, $1.32, 10 m 54 s, 61% of written tokens thinking, 10 claims, 9 arrows of which 8 documented, 0 refused, stopped at `width_cap`**. The same line notes "No Sonnet number is quoted anywhere in this chapter, because none has been measured yet" — though `docs/measurements.md:48-67` now carries two Sonnet Hormuz runs from 2026-09-21, so the chapter is one day stale on that point.

ADR-0015's side of the contract: `docs/adr/0015-a-claim-starts-with-the-range-the-model-stated.md:72` ("**The eval scorecard is the baseline.**"), `:101` (the confirmation item), and `:10` (spec-impact line). The reopening route is scorecard → pastcast → measure whether re-asking widens ranges toward the truth.

**The gap worth naming:** the baseline is fully specified and entirely unpopulated. `evals/runs/` holds no TSV, `docs/measurements.md:40-44` points at a scorecard that does not exist, and `evaluation.md:218` requires "All four cases run once through it as soon as the pipeline is green (Kent, G6)". **One sentence: freeze the answer shapes once, record once, buy the latency cheaply, and make

### 2.1 The shape freeze (stack 05, top)

Everything that changes `STANDING_TEXT` or `what_goes_out()` moves the prompt fingerprint
(`prompt.py:154`), and a moved fingerprint fails `check_recordings` and costs a paid re-record
(~$4, ~40 min) plus a cassette re-record (~$1). So they go in **one commit, once**:

```python
class LinkDraft(BaseModel):
    mode: Literal["trigger", "sustain"]
    p_effect_if_cause: float      # P(effect | cause), plain probability
    p_effect_if_not_cause: float  # P(effect | not cause)
    lag: int
    shape: Literal["impulse", "step", "ramp"]
    half_life: int | None = None
    rationale: str
    what_would_change_my_mind: str     # one named observable
    sources: tuple[SourceDraft, ...] = ()

class SourceDraft(BaseModel):
    url: str
    quote: str   # the sentence on that page that carries the weight
    role: Literal["mechanism", "magnitude", "timing", "resolution", "instrument"]
```

Our code keeps every decision it already owns: it mints ids, stamps `owner="model"`, computes
`strength = logit(q₁) − logit(q₀)` (clipped, with the clip reported), sets the leak to `q₀`, decides
`documented`/`argued` from what the search returned, and now also records whether the quote's page was
reachable. **Removed**: `strength` as an elicited field, and with it the "+1 triples the odds" anchor.
Also in the freeze: `kind` required on both payoff shapes (the branch already written); the three
inhibitor/falsifier sentences; the "do not search on the first call" rule; the thin-base-rate rule.

**Then, and only then, re-record Hormuz once.** Everything else waits behind it.

### 2.2 Latency, bought cheaply

Two changes, measured, ~40 lines: the starting call does not search (**7 s** to the first tile,
measured) and `at_once` goes 3 → 5 (measured parallelism is already 1.5× at 3). At `EFFORT=medium`
that is a first tile at ~15 s and a whole map in ~5 minutes for $1.31 — which is what a live user
gets. The recordings stay at default effort (G13 stands).

### 2.3 Skeleton-first: a bet, not a premise (stack 06)

Its quality argument is measurably dead — the walk already draws DAGs with up to four parents. Its
remaining case is **more map per minute** and a first tile that arrives while a human is still
reading the hypothesis. Priced against the measurements, not the sketch: **≈$2.0–2.6 and ≈5–6
minutes** for 15–18 claims, first tile ~20 s *and only if we build a streaming JSON path that does
not exist today*. Compare: today's medium-effort run with §2.2's fixes is ~5 minutes and $1.31 for
9–12 claims. So it buys size and first-paint, not wall clock, for about twice the money and 2.5–3
sessions.

Build it as **one decision per proposal, with proposals arriving in batches** — `grow.py` stays the
one walk driver, each element in the skeleton folds through the same `_judge` on the same candidate
map, and each emits the same `proposal_accepted` / `proposal_rejected` with a rising `at`, so the
recording grammar, replay and reject-never-repair all survive untouched. Amends ADR-0006's *"one
call per proposal"* to *"one decision per proposal"*. **Kill criterion, decided on the scorecard:**
if a skeleton round does not beat the walk on `claims`, `inhibiting_links` and `source_support_rate`
at equal or lower dollars, it is deleted and the walk stands.

### 2.4 Evidence (stack 05, with the fetch-check in 06)

The smallest change that gets most of the value is the two fields above plus an Inspector that reads
*quote → role → link*, and **the showcase's trade-critical sources checked by hand once** — which is
what both reviews actually ask for. Review2's automatic check cannot be built: the service returns
`encrypted_content`, not text, and the structured answer carries no `citations`. The honest automatic
version is **our own** fetch of the cited page and a substring match — the same shape of rule as
`keep_cited`, and a fourth word a reader can trust. It belongs in 06 because it adds a network step
to generation that replay must never need.

### 2.5 Evaluation (counts in 05, rubric in 07)

Add the seven counting columns to the existing scorecard — they cost nothing and they are exactly the
properties that changed between 09-17 and today, so they are what a regression would show. Keep the
house rule that **no model grades a model**. The content questions both reviews want are graded by
**a person, once per round**, on a printed sheet of 10 maps × 6 axes: resolvable · mechanism specific
· source supports the claim · DAG not tree · priced-in named · observation versus intervention. One
afternoon. Put it in stack 07 beside the pastcast — and **prefer the rubric to the pastcast**: the
pastcast needs a date-frozen corpus we do not have, and review/ 10:31 warns that a binary Brier score
cannot validate an interval over a latent probability anyway. The rubric is the cheaper instrument
and it answers the question Kent actually has.

### 2.6 Interactive verbs (stack 06) — and what stack 06 is now FOR

Stack 06 stops being "probes" and becomes **the map you can argue with**: *expand this claim* ·
*challenge this arrow* · *add an event* (built, one live run from proven), ranked by *spend here*
(already computed). *Challenge this arrow* **is** the role-played expert FR-9 permits and the red-team
call review2 wants — one feature where the roadmap had two. Cut: `refine`/INV-10, reflexive-loop
unrolling, the random-simulation probe.

**Records amended:** ADR-0006 (one *decision* per proposal; the research budget narrowed), ADR-0003's
2026-09-17 amendment (unchanged — three silent retries stand), ADR-0015 (the coherence residual now;
k = 3 only if the scorecard earns it; G1's *"nothing extra in a recording"* is what an ensemble would
break, and it must be said out loud), ADR-0010 (a source carries a passage and a role), ADR-0013
(`kind` required). PRD anti-pattern 2 gains one clarifying clause.

> passage on every source. **Recommendation: land the recording you already have, hold the payoff fix
> and the cassette re-record until all the shape changes land together, then record once.** Cost:
> $0 now, ~$5 and ~45 minutes once, in stack 05. The alternative — record now and again later — is
> ~$10 and ~90 minutes for the same result. There is no risk in waiting: the payoff defect is latent
> (the model filled the field anyway in all eleven of the recording's trades).

**2. The number on an arrow becomes two probabilities.**

> Today the model writes an abstract "strength", and the description we send it says "+1 triples the

> effect if the cause happens?* and *how likely if it does not?* Our code turns those into the same
> arrow. On screen the Inspector stops saying "strength 2.2" and starts saying **"war-risk premiums
> falling takes Brent below $68 from 31% to 64%"** — a sentence a trader can disagree with. It also
> gives us a free honesty check: the model's three numbers around each arrow must roughly agree, and
> we can show by how much they do not. Cost: ~0.7 session and it rides the one re-record above.
> Option B: keep `strength` and only bound it. Cheaper by half a session; keeps the anchor we wrote.

**3. Skeleton-first is a bet with a kill switch, not a foregone conclusion.**

> Measured on your own recording, that is no longer true: the map already has claims with two and
> four causes, and the run before the recording drew three arrows that push *down*. What one big call
> would still buy is a first tile in about twenty seconds instead of a minute or two, and a bigger
> map for the same wait. Priced honestly it is about **$2.0–2.6 and five to six minutes** — roughly
> twice today's money at medium effort — and 2.5–3 sessions of work including a streaming path we do
> not have. **Recommendation: buy the cheap 90% first** (the first call does not search — measured at
> 7 seconds — and five lines grow at once), then build the big call in stack 06 and delete it if it
> does not beat the walk on the scorecard. Option B: build it in 05, before the thesis. It is the one
> thing here that could eat a week.

**4. Twenty-five searches a claim: keep, narrow, or drop.**

> You decided the model should research its reference class, up to 25 searches a claim. Measured:
> 93 searches on the Hormuz recording produced **five** base rates across eighteen claims, and three
> of those five are "0 out of 2", "2 out of 3" and "1 out of 1" — which are not reference classes.
> A call that searches takes three to four times as long as one that does not, so this is where most
> of the thirty-six minutes went. **Recommendation: research only where a reference class can exist**
> — not on the first call, not on a price threshold — and drop a count with fewer than five cases
> rather than print "1 of 1". Cost: ~0.3 session; saves roughly a third of the clock.

**5. Who grades quality — and is a rubric better value than a pastcast?**

> Today's evals count shapes: no loops, every arrow has a reason, every trade names an instrument.
> They cannot see that a source does not say what we cite it for. **Recommendation: you, or one
> person, once a round** — ten maps, six questions each, on one printed page, one afternoon. No model
> ever grades another model. That is worth more than the pastcast in stack 07, which needs a corpus
> frozen before each event that we do not have, and whose score cannot actually test the thing we
> would want tested. Cost: half a session to build, one afternoon per round. Option B: pastcast
> first — a stronger public claim if it works, one-and-a-half sessions plus the corpus problem.

**6. Stack 06 changes what it is for.**

> It was "probes": split a claim into finer claims, run simulations on one node, role-play experts,
> unroll feedback loops. Both reviews say cut all of that. **Recommendation: stack 06 becomes the map
> you can argue with** — *expand this claim*, *challenge this arrow*, *add an event*, each ranked by
> the "spend here" number the engine already computes and nobody can see. The role-played expert
> survives as *challenge this arrow*, which is the honest version of it. What that costs you: the

## 2. The design I recommend

**One sentence: freeze the answer shapes once, record once, buy the latency cheaply, and make
skeleton-first a measured bet in stack 06 rather than an article of faith.**

### 2.1 The shape freeze (stack 05, top)

Everything that changes `STANDING_TEXT` or `what_goes_out()` moves the prompt fingerprint
(`prompt.py:154`), and a moved fingerprint fails `check_recordings` and costs a paid re-record
(~$4, ~40 min) plus a cassette re-record (~$1). So they go in **one commit, once**:

```python
class LinkDraft(BaseModel):
    mode: Literal["trigger", "sustain"]
    p_effect_if_cause: float      # P(effect | cause), plain probability
    p_effect_if_not_cause: float  # P(effect | not cause)
    lag: int
    shape: Literal["impulse", "step", "ramp"]
    half_life: int | None = None
    rationale: str
    what_would_change_my_mind: str     # one named observable
    sources: tuple[SourceDraft, ...] = ()

class SourceDraft(BaseModel):
    url: str
    quote: str   # the sentence on that page that carries the weight
    role: Literal["mechanism", "magnitude", "timing", "resolution", "instrument"]
```

Our code keeps every decision it already owns: it mints ids, stamps `owner="model"`, computes
`strength = logit(q₁) − logit(q₀)` (clipped, with the clip reported), sets the leak to `q₀`, decides
`documented`/`argued` from what the search returned, and now also records whether the quote's page was
reachable. **Removed**: `strength` as an elicited field, and with it the "+1 triples the odds" anchor.
Also in the freeze: `kind` required on both payoff shapes (the branch already written); the three
inhibitor/falsifier sentences; the "do not search on the first call" rule; the thin-base-rate rule.

**Then, and only then, re-record Hormuz once.** Everything else waits behind it.

### 2.2 Latency, bought cheaply

Two changes, measured, ~40 lines: the starting call does not search (**7 s** to the first tile,
measured) and `at_once` goes 3 → 5 (measured parallelism is already 1.5× at 3). At `EFFORT=medium`
that is a first tile at ~15 s and a whole map in ~5 minutes for $1.31 — which is what a live user
gets. The recordings stay at default effort (G13 stands).

### 2.3 Skeleton-first: a bet, not a premise (stack 06)

Its quality argument is measurably dead — the walk already draws DAGs with up to four parents. Its
remaining case is **more map per minute** and a first tile that arrives while a human is still
reading the hypothesis. Priced against the measurements, not the sketch: **≈$2.0–2.6 and ≈5–6
minutes** for 15–18 claims, first tile ~20 s *and only if we build a streaming JSON path that does
not exist today*. Compare: today's medium-effort run with §2.2's fixes is ~5 minutes and $1.31 for
9–12 claims. So it buys size and first-paint, not wall clock, for about twice the money and 2.5–3
sessions.

Build it as **one decision per proposal, with proposals arriving in batches** — `grow.py` stays the
one walk driver, each element in the skeleton folds through the same `_judge` on the same candidate
map, and each emits the same `proposal_accepted` / `proposal_rejected` with a rising `at`, so the
recording grammar, replay and reject-never-repair all survive untouched. Amends ADR-0006's *"one
call per proposal"* to *"one decision per proposal"*. **Kill criterion, decided on the scorecard:**
if a skeleton round does not beat the walk on `claims`, `inhibiting_links` and `source_support_rate`
at equal or lower dollars, it is deleted and the walk stands.

### 2.4 Evidence (stack 05, with the fetch-check in 06)

The smallest change that gets most of the value is the two fields above plus an Inspector that reads
*quote → role → link*, and **the showcase's trade-critical sources checked by hand once** — which is
what both reviews actually ask for. Review2's automatic check cannot be built: the service returns
`encrypted_content`, not text, and the structured answer carries no `citations`. The honest automatic
version is **our own** fetch of the cited page and a substring match — the same shape of rule as
`keep_cited`, and a fourth word a reader can trust. It belongs in 06 because it adds a network step
to generation that replay must never need.

### 2.5 Evaluation (counts in 05, rubric in 07)

Add the seven counting columns to the existing scorecard — they cost nothing and they are exactly the
properties that changed between 09-17 and today, so they are what a regression would show. Keep the
house rule that **no model grades a model**. The content questions both reviews want are graded by
**a person, once per round**, on a printed sheet of 10 maps × 6 axes: resolvable · mechanism specific
· source supports the claim · DAG not tree · priced-in named · observation versus intervention. One
afternoon. Put it in stack 07 beside the pastcast — and **prefer the rubric to the pastcast**: the
pastcast needs a date-frozen corpus we do not have, and review/ 10:31 warns that a binary Brier score
cannot validate an interval over a latent probability anyway. The rubric is the cheaper instrument
and it answers the question Kent actually has.

### 2.6 Interactive verbs (stack 06) — and what stack 06 is now FOR

Stack 06 stops being "probes" and becomes **the map you can argue with**: *expand this claim* ·
*challenge this arrow* · *add an event* (built, one live run from proven), ranked by *spend here*
(already computed). *Challenge this arrow* **is** the role-played expert FR-9 permits and the red-team
call review2 wants — one feature where the roadmap had two. Cut: `refine`/INV-10, reflexive-loop
unrolling, the random-simulation probe.

**Records amended:** ADR-0006 (one *decision* per proposal; the research budget narrowed), ADR-0003's
2026-09-17 amendment (unchanged — three silent retries stand), ADR-0015 (the coherence residual now;

> and the cassette re-record until all the shape changes land together, then record once.** Cost:

> — not on the first call, not on a price threshold — and drop a count with fewer than five cases
> rather than print "1 of 1". Cost: ~0.3 session; saves roughly a third of the clock.

> ever grades another model. That is worth more than the pastcast in stack 07, which needs a corpus
> frozen before each event that we do not have, and whose score cannot actually test the thing we
> would want tested. Cost: half a session to build, one afternoon per round. Option B: pastcast

Four measured facts that change the argument:

1. **The map is no longer a tree.** `LinkProposal` — the shape review2 says is never used — is used in

2. **A call that searches costs 3–4× the seconds of one that does not.** Default effort: median

3. **G7's research budget bought thin reference classes.** 93 searches produced **5** base rates on 18

## 2. The design I recommend

**One sentence: freeze the answer shapes once, record once, buy the latency cheaply, and make
skeleton-first a measured bet in stack 06 rather than an article of faith.**

### 2.1 The shape freeze (stack 05, top)

Everything that changes `STANDING_TEXT` or `what_goes_out()` moves the prompt fingerprint
(`prompt.py:154`), and a moved fingerprint fails `check_recordings` and costs a paid re-record
(~$4, ~40 min) plus a cassette re-record (~$1). So they go in **one commit, once**:

```python
class LinkDraft(BaseModel):
    mode: Literal["trigger", "sustain"]
    p_effect_if_cause: float      # P(effect | cause), plain probability
    p_effect_if_not_cause: float  # P(effect | not cause)
    lag: int
    shape: Literal["impulse", "step", "ramp"]
    half_life: int | None = None
    rationale: str
    what_would_change_my_mind: str     # one named observable
    sources: tuple[SourceDraft, ...] = ()

class SourceDraft(BaseModel):
    url: str
    quote: str   # the sentence on that page that carries the weight
    role: Literal["mechanism", "magnitude", "timing", "resolution", "instrument"]
```

Our code keeps every decision it already owns: it mints ids, stamps `owner="model"`, computes
`strength = logit(q₁) − logit(q₀)` (clipped, with the clip reported), sets the leak to `q₀`, decides
`documented`/`argued` from what the search returned, and now also records whether the quote's page was
reachable. **Removed**: `strength` as an elicited field, and with it the "+1 triples the odds" anchor.
Also in the freeze: `kind` required on both payoff shapes (the branch already written); the three
inhibitor/falsifier sentences; the "do not search on the first call" rule; the thin-base-rate rule.

**Then, and only then, re-record Hormuz once.** Everything else waits behind it.

### 2.2 Latency, bought cheaply

Two changes, measured, ~40 lines: the starting call does not search (**7 s** to the first tile,
measured) and `at_once` goes 3 → 5 (measured parallelism is already 1.5× at 3). At `EFFORT=medium`
that is a first tile at ~15 s and a whole map in ~5 minutes for $1.31 — which is what a live user
gets. The recordings stay at default effort (G13 stands).

### 2.3 Skeleton-first: a bet, not a premise (stack 06)

Its quality argument is measurably dead — the walk already draws DAGs with up to four parents. Its
remaining case is **more map per minute** and a first tile that arrives while a human is still
reading the hypothesis. Priced against the measurements, not the sketch: **≈$2.0–2.6 and ≈5–6
minutes** for 15–18 claims, first tile ~20 s *and only if we build a streaming JSON path that does
not exist today*. Compare: today's medium-effort run with §2.2's fixes is ~5 minutes and $1.31 for
9–12 claims. So it buys size and first-paint, not wall clock, for about twice the money and 2.5–3
sessions.

Build it as **one decision per proposal, with proposals arriving in batches** — `grow.py` stays the
one walk driver, each element in the skeleton folds through the same `_judge` on the same candidate
map, and each emits the same `proposal_accepted` / `proposal_rejected` with a rising `at`, so the
recording grammar, replay and reject-never-repair all survive untouched. Amends ADR-0006's *"one
call per proposal"* to *"one decision per proposal"*. **Kill criterion, decided on the scorecard:**
if a skeleton round does not beat the walk on `claims`, `inhibiting_links` and `source_support_rate`
at equal or lower dollars, it is deleted and the walk stands.

### 2.4 Evidence (stack 05, with the fetch-check in 06)

The smallest change that gets most of the value is the two fields above plus an Inspector that reads
*quote → role → link*, and **the showcase's trade-critical sources checked by hand once** — which is
what both reviews actually ask for. Review2's automatic check cannot be built: the service returns
`encrypted_content`, not text, and the structured answer carries no `citations`. The honest automatic
version is **our own** fetch of the cited page and a substring match — the same shape of rule as
`keep_cited`, and a fourth word a reader can trust. It belongs in 06 because it adds a network step
to generation that replay must never need.

### 2.5 Evaluation (counts in 05, rubric in 07)

Add the seven counting columns to the existing scorecard — they cost nothing and they are exactly the
properties that changed between 09-17 and today, so they are what a regression would show. Keep the
house rule that **no model grades a model**. The content questions both reviews want are graded by
**a person, once per round**, on a printed sheet of 10 maps × 6 axes: resolvable · mechanism specific
· source supports the claim · DAG not tree · priced-in named · observation versus intervention. One
afternoon. Put it in stack 07 beside the pastcast — and **prefer the rubric to the pastcast**: the
pastcast needs a date-frozen corpus we do not have, and review/ 10:31 warns that a binary Brier score
cannot validate an interval over a latent probability anyway. The rubric is the cheaper instrument
and it answers the question Kent actually has.

### 2.6 Interactive verbs (stack 06) — and what stack 06 is now FOR

Stack 06 stops being "probes" and becomes **the map you can argue with**: *expand this claim* ·
*challenge this arrow* · *add an event* (built, one live run from proven), ranked by *spend here*
(already computed). *Challenge this arrow* **is** the role-played expert FR-9 permits and the red-team
call review2 wants — one feature where the roadmap had two. Cut: `refine`/INV-10, reflexive-loop
unrolling, the random-simulation probe.

**Records amended:** ADR-0006 (one *decision* per proposal; the research budget narrowed), ADR-0003's
2026-09-17 amendment (unchanged — three silent retries stand), ADR-0015 (the coherence residual now;
k = 3 only if the scorecard earns it; G1's *"nothing extra in a recording"* is what an ensemble would
break, and it must be said out loud), ADR-0010 (a source carries a passage and a role), ADR-0013
(`kind` required). PRD anti-pattern 2 gains one clarifying clause.

| 06-G4 | **Spend here** — a route and the Inspector sentence for `World.range_shares`, with review/'s caveat on screen | +130 | 0.7 sess |
| 06-G5 | **Skeleton-first, gated.** One streamed structured call drafts a *thin* skeleton (sentence · kind · arrows), enrichment in parallel per element, one red-team call. Batched proposals, one decision each, same `_judge`, same events. **Kill criterion on the scorecard** | +650 −200 | 2.5–3 sess |
| 06-G6 | **The fetch-and-substring check** on cited pages (G-e fuller) | +120 | 0.5 sess |
| **Not done in 06, and why** | `refine` + INV-10 (**CUT** — more detail need not preserve the marginal; the invariant is satisfied by a named refusal) · reflexive-loop unrolling (**CUT** — a simulation law the assignment does not ask for) · the random-simulation probe (**CUT** — the band already comes from the engine) · autonomous agent society (anti-pattern 7) | | |

### Stack 07 — *how we know a map is any good* (generation share: ~1.5 sessions + human time)

| Order | Work | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| 07-G1 | **The hand rubric** — 10 hypotheses (the brief's four plus six the prompt has never seen) × 6 axes, scored 0–2 by a person on a printed sheet, notes kept beside each saved case. Built once, run per round | 0.4 sess + **one human afternoon per round**, ~$5–20 of model spend per round |
| 07-G2 | **The ensemble decision, on numbers** — k = 3 on the arrows into tradeable endings only, geometric mean of odds, **the raw samples kept in the recording**, judged on the rubric and the counting columns against the 05 baseline. Reject if flat | 0.7 sess, ~$1–2 a round |
| 07-G3 | **The other three recordings** — only on Kent's explicit word | ~$15, ~2 h |
| 07-G4 | Pastcast — **only if appetite remains after the rubric.** It needs a date-frozen corpus that does not exist, and a Brier score on a binary outcome cannot validate an interval over a latent probability | 1.5+ sess |
| **Not done, and why** | a model grading a model (Kent vetoes it, and both reviews agree the rubric must be human) · calibration fitting (nothing has resolved) · extremizing (research-A: LLM samples are correlated; it manufactures confidence) | |

---

## 6. Decisions that are genuinely Kent's

**1. The Hormuz re-recording: wait, or pay twice.** *(recommended first)*

> Your Hormuz recording cost $4 and 36 minutes. Making the payoff `kind` required changes what we ask
> the model for, so the recording no longer matches what ships and the build says to record it again.
> Stack 05 will change what we ask for a second time — conditional numbers on the arrows, a quoted
> passage on every source. **Recommendation: land the recording you already have, hold the payoff fix
> and the cassette re-record until all the shape changes land together, then record once.** Cost:
> $0 now, ~$5 and ~45 minutes once, in stack 05. The alternative — record now and again later — is
> ~$10 and ~90 minutes for the same result. There is no risk in waiting: the payoff defect is latent
> (the model filled the field anyway in all eleven of the recording's trades).

**2. The number on an arrow becomes two probabilities.**

> Today the model writes an abstract "strength", and the description we send it says "+1 triples the
> odds" — a number we invented, in a prompt. Instead we ask two plain questions: *how likely is the
> effect if the cause happens?* and *how likely if it does not?* Our code turns those into the same
> arrow. On screen the Inspector stops saying "strength 2.2" and starts saying **"war-risk premiums
> falling takes Brent below $68 from 31% to 64%"** — a sentence a trader can disagree with. It also
> gives us a free honesty check: the model's three numbers around each arrow must roughly agree, and
> we can show by how much they do not. Cost: ~0.7 session and it rides the one re-record above.
> Option B: keep `strength` and only bound it. Cheaper by half a session; keeps the anchor we wrote.

**3. Skeleton-first is a bet with a kill switch, not a foregone conclusion.**

> The review said drawing the whole map in one call is the *only* way to get a claim with two causes.
> Measured on your own recording, that is no longer true: the map already has claims with two and
> four causes, and the run before the recording drew three arrows that push *down*. What one big call
> would still buy is a first tile in about twenty seconds instead of a minute or two, and a bigger
> map for the same wait. Priced honestly it is about **$2.0–2.6 and five to six minutes** — roughly
> twice today's money at medium effort — and 2.5–3 sessions of work including a streaming path we do
> not have. **Recommendation: buy the cheap 90% first** (the first call does not search — measured at
> 7 seconds — and five lines grow at once), then build the big call in stack 06 and delete it if it
> does not beat the walk on the scorecard. Option B: build it in 05, before the thesis. It is the one
> thing here that could eat a week.

**4. Twenty-five searches a claim: keep, narrow, or drop.**

> You decided the model should research its reference class, up to 25 searches a claim. Measured:
> 93 searches on the Hormuz recording produced **five** base rates across eighteen claims, and three
> of those five are "0 out of 2", "2 out of 3" and "1 out of 1" — which are not reference classes.
> A call that searches takes three to four times as long as one that does not, so this is where most
> of the thirty-six minutes went. **Recommendation: research only where a reference class can exist**
> — not on the first call, not on a price threshold — and drop a count with fewer than five cases
> rather than print "1 of 1". Cost: ~0.3 session; saves roughly a third of the clock.

**5. Who grades quality — and is a rubric better value than a pastcast?**

> Today's evals count shapes: no loops, every arrow has a reason, every trade names an instrument.
> They cannot see that a source does not say what we cite it for. **Recommendation: you, or one
> person, once a round** — ten maps, six questions each, on one printed page, one afternoon. No model
> ever grades another model. That is worth more than the pastcast in stack 07, which needs a corpus
> frozen before each event that we do not have, and whose score cannot actually test the thing we
> would want tested. Cost: half a session to build, one afternoon per round. Option B: pastcast
> first — a stronger public claim if it works, one-and-a-half sessions plus the corpus problem.

**6. Stack 06 changes what it is for.**

> It was "probes": split a claim into finer claims, run simulations on one node, role-play experts,
> unroll feedback loops. Both reviews say cut all of that. **Recommendation: stack 06 becomes the map
> you can argue with** — *expand this claim*, *challenge this arrow*, *add an event*, each ranked by
> the "spend here" number the engine already computes and nobody can see. The role-played expert
> survives as *challenge this arrow*, which is the honest version of it. What that costs you: the
> chess-engine analogy you liked. What it buys: the brief's audit clause, and the one inhibiting
> arrow the showcase map does not have.

---

## 7. What I did not check

- **I did not call a model or spend a cent**, so every latency and cost figure for anything not yet
  built is arithmetic over the measured runs, not a measurement. In particular the skeleton-first
  numbers (≈$2.0–2.6, ≈5–6 min, ~20 s first tile) rest on the measured 55 output-tokens/second and
  $0.139/call, and on a guess at how many tokens a thin skeleton is. A one-call spike would settle it
  for about $0.20.
- **I did not run the test suites, the browser, or `make eval`.** The evals findings come from
  reading `evals/run.py` and `spec/generation/evaluation.md` on `feat/04b-evals`, not from a round.
- **I did not verify that a streaming structured call can be recorded by the cassette layer.** VCR
  and streamed responses are awkward together; that is unquantified risk on 06-G5.
- **I did not check any source in any map by hand.** The claim that the recording's evidence is thin
  rests on the shape of `Source` (url, title, date — no passage), not on opening thirty-seven pages.
  Checking the trade-critical ones is itself one of my recommendations.
- **I did not read the frontend Inspector code**, so my line estimates for its changes (~40–80 lines
  each) are the weakest numbers here. CRAFT owns that surface.
- **I did not price the rate-limit risk** of running 12–37 enrichment calls concurrently against the
  service.
- **The engine's two reproduced defects are ENGINE's**, not mine; I assumed their fixes land and do
  not change the generation shapes. If the engine's reformulation changes what an arrow *is*, my
  "freeze the shapes once" plan absorbs it — but only if it lands before 05-G1.

Report written to `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/analysis/2026-09-21-digest-generation.md`.

**Summary (~300 words)**

I measured the committed Hormuz recording and the three kept runs before judging anything. Two of review2's central generation claims are already dead. The map is **not a tree**: 1.12–1.37 links per claim, two claims with two parents in the recording, one with four in the 09-21 run, and `LinkProposal` — the shape review2 says is never used — accounts for 2 of 20 and 7 of 28 accepted proposals. So *"`ClaimProposal`'s single `cause` is why the map is a tree"* is false, and with it the main **quality** argument for skeleton-first. Its remaining case is latency: first tile 67–135 s, first complete chain 95–611 s, whole map 36 min, $4.04 (29 calls, 93 searches). Priced against $0.139/call and 55 output-tokens/s, review2's "~3 min, ~$0.70" is roughly 2× optimistic on time and 3× on cost — realistically $2.0–2.6 and 5–6 min, and 20 s to first tile *only* with a streaming path that does not exist. A searchless first call gives 7 s, measured. Skeleton-first belongs in 06 with a kill criterion, not in 05.

G7 is the clock: searching calls take 3–4× the seconds and bought 5 base rates on 18 claims, three of them `0/2`, `2/3`, `1/1`. Review2's evidence fix cannot be built — the service returns `encrypted_content`, and the structured answer carries no citations; review/'s passage-plus-support-role is right.

**The coordinator's held question, answered: do not re-record.** Land the existing recording, hold `fix/04-payoff-kind-required` and the cassette re-record, batch every shape change (conditional q₀/q₁, source quote+role, payoff `kind`, the missing inhibitor sentences) into one freeze at the top of 05, then record once — $5 instead of $10. The defect is latent; all eleven payoffs read back fine.

Also found: `make eval`'s $15 cap is per case, so a four-case round can spend $60.
